title: Early human migration

match.reason: The Out of Africa card covers the core idea of migration out of Africa, but it presents the theory as the scientific consensus and never teaches that the routes and timing are still debated, which the new point requires.

draft.title: Early human migration
card: Modern humans, called Homo sapiens, first lived in Africa. Over tens of thousands of years, groups moved out and spread to other parts of the world.
People moved for reasons such as finding food, following animals, or responding to changes in climate. They travelled on foot and, in some places, by boat.
Our evidence comes from bones, stone tools and the remains of camps. Scientists also study the DNA of people today and of ancient remains.
Historians and scientists still debate the routes and the timing. New finds can change what they think.
draft.remember: Humans began in Africa and spread out over a very long time. The routes and dates are still debated.

a.q: Where did modern humans, Homo sapiens, first live?
opts: Africa
Europe
Asia
Australia
a.why: The evidence shows that Homo sapiens first lived in Africa and then spread to other regions. Europe, Asia and Australia were reached later by groups who moved out over a very long time.
a.clue: Think about where the spread began.

b.q: A team in a cave finds human bones that look older than any found before in the region. Some experts say the spread of humans must have begun earlier. What does this show?
opts: New finds can change ideas about the timing
The debate about migration has now ended
Humans did not begin in Africa after all
Humans only travelled by boat in this region
b.why: The card says new finds can change what experts think, so one find may lead them to rethink the timing. A single find does not end the debate or overturn the African origin of modern humans.
b.clue: Think about what new evidence does to existing ideas.

wants.brief: A world map showing Africa as the starting point of modern humans, with arrows spreading out towards Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas. Label the continents. Arrows should be marked as approximate routes.
wants.why: It helps students see the direction of the spread from Africa across the world.

b.best: New finds can change ideas about the timing

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('can change'). The three distractors are all absolute claims ('has now ended', 'only travelled by boat', 'did not begin in Africa after all'), so a student could pick the answer by spotting the odd one out without knowing the idea.

The stem has experts say the spread 'must have begun earlier' from a single find. This is firmer than the card, which stresses that the timing is debated and that finds 'can' change ideas. 'May have begun earlier' would fit the card better.
